lesson.title: Look Before You Differentiate: Simplifying First
lesson.summary: Splitting a fraction, expanding a product, or applying a logarithm property before differentiating often turns a messy product or quotient rule problem into a quick linear combination instead.
lesson.body:
Not every expression that looks like it needs the product rule or quotient rule actually does. Before reaching for a combining rule, it is worth pausing to ask whether basic algebra, factoring, expanding, splitting a fraction into separate terms, or applying a logarithm or exponent law, can rewrite the expression into something with a much simpler structure. Simplifying first is not cheating, it is often the fastest and least error prone route to the correct derivative.

Consider f(x) = (x^3 + 2x) / x. Applying the quotient rule directly works, but it is more work than necessary. Instead, split the fraction term by term: (x^3 + 2x)/x = x^2 + 2. Now the derivative is immediate by the power rule: f'(x) = 2x. As a check, apply the quotient rule to the original form anyway: with numerator derivative 3x^2 + 2 and denominator derivative 1, the quotient rule gives [(3x^2 + 2)(x) - (x^3 + 2x)(1)] / x^2 = [3x^3 + 2x - x^3 - 2x] / x^2 = 2x^3 / x^2 = 2x. Both routes agree, but the simplified version got there in one line.

Logarithm properties are especially powerful simplifiers. Differentiate g(x) = ln(x^3 e^x). Rather than treating this as a single complicated composition, use the log rule that turns a product inside a logarithm into a sum outside it: ln(x^3 e^x) = ln(x^3) + ln(e^x) = 3 ln x + x, since ln(e^x) equals x by definition of inverse functions. Now differentiate this simplified sum directly: g'(x) = 3/x + 1. Splitting the logarithm first avoided any need for more advanced tools and reduced the whole problem to rules you already have.

Expanding a product can help just as much. Differentiate p(x) = (e^x - 1)(e^x + 1). Recognize the difference of squares pattern: (e^x - 1)(e^x + 1) = (e^x)^2 - 1 = e^(2x) - 1. Using the scaled exponential rule from earlier, the derivative of e^(2x) is 2e^(2x), and the derivative of the constant -1 is 0, so p'(x) = 2e^(2x). Compare this against differentiating the unexpanded product directly with the product rule: p'(x) = e^x(e^x + 1) + (e^x - 1)e^x = e^(2x) + e^x + e^(2x) - e^x = 2e^(2x). The two methods match exactly, but the expanded version required far less bookkeeping.

The general habit worth building is to scan an expression before differentiating for factorable structure, products of binomials that expand into a difference of squares or simpler polynomial, fractions that split term by term, and logarithm or exponent laws that turn products, quotients, or powers inside a log into sums, differences, or constant multiples outside it. A few seconds of algebra up front routinely saves several lines of derivative rule bookkeeping and reduces the chance of an arithmetic slip, and as later sections introduce the chain rule, this same instinct to simplify first will often mean the difference between a one layer computation and a needlessly nested one.
